title: Direct air capture cost curve to $100 per tonne
bottleneck: Direct air capture today costs on the order of $600-1,500 per tonne of CO2, roughly ten times the $100 target that would make it a plausible climate tool. Costs are dominated by energy, capital-intensive contactors, and sorbent replacement, and unlike solar panels, DAC plants are bespoke chemical facilities with limited learning-curve evidence. No credible, demonstrated pathway shows costs falling an order of magnitude within the needed timeframe.
why_it_blocks: At current costs, removing even 1 gigatonne a year would cost around a trillion dollars annually — politically and economically impossible. The cost gap means DAC functions as an expensive offset for the wealthy rather than a scalable climate solution.
current_state: Optimistic roadmaps assume $150 per tonne by 2050 through scale and learning, and the Texas Stratos plant aims at 500,000 tonnes a year. But as one analysis notes, even that optimistic cost implies $1.5 trillion a year for 10 gigatonnes, and real-world plants like Climeworks' Iceland facilities have underperformed their nameplate capture.
